question: What should I do if I experience skin reactions like rashes or itching during chemotherapy?
derived_answer: Skin reactions such as rashes, itching, redness, or changes in skin color can sometimes occur as a side effect of chemotherapy. If you develop any skin irritation or rashes anywhere on your body during treatment, it's important to mention this to your treatment team right away. They can monitor the symptoms and prescribe medication to help alleviate the skin reaction if needed. Don't hesitate to report any concerning skin changes, as your healthcare team wants to help manage any side effects you may experience. With proper treatment, many skin reactions can be controlled or minimized.

question: What precautions should I take when using anti-inflammatory pain medication during chemotherapy?
derived_answer: Before taking any anti-inflammatory pain relief medication during your chemotherapy treatment, it's important to consult with your treatment team first. They can advise you on the correct dosage, how long you should use the medication, and any potential side effects or interactions to be aware of. This is especially crucial if you have pre-existing conditions like stomach ulcers or asthma, as anti-inflammatory drugs may exacerbate those conditions. Your healthcare providers want to ensure the pain medication is safe and effective for your specific situation, so always check with them before using anti-inflammatory pain relievers.

question: What is hand-foot syndrome and how can it be treated?
derived_answer: Hand-foot syndrome, also known as palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, is a skin reaction that can occur as a side effect of certain chemotherapy drugs like docetaxel. It usually affects the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but may also involve other areas like the knees or elbows. This condition can make daily activities more difficult and impact your quality of life. Your treatment team may prescribe gels or creams to apply to the affected areas to help manage the symptoms. It's important to consult with them before using any products on your skin during treatment. You can find more information about hand-foot syndrome on the Breast Cancer Now website.

question: How can docetaxel affect my nails?
derived_answer: Docetaxel chemotherapy can cause changes to your fingernails and toenails. You may notice differences in their color or texture, or the development of ridges in the nails. The nails may also become more brittle and prone to cracking. In some cases, the nail may even lift off the nail bed and fall out, although it will grow back eventually. Since chemotherapy increases your risk of infection, it's important to report any signs of infection like redness, heat, swelling or pain in or under your nails to your treatment team right away.

question: How can I take care of my mouth during chemotherapy?
derived_answer: Taking good care of your mouth, teeth and gums is very important during chemotherapy treatment. Your treatment team may provide you with a special mouthwash to help reduce soreness and prevent mouth ulcers from developing. It's a good idea to use a small, soft-bristled toothbrush during this time to be gentle on your mouth. Before starting chemotherapy, it's recommended to visit your dentist for a check-up. Try to avoid any dental work during your treatments if possible. However, if you do need dental work, discuss the best timing with your treatment team. For more detailed information on coping with a sore mouth during chemotherapy, refer to the 'Chemotherapy for breast cancer' booklet.

question: What can I do if my sense of taste changes while taking docetaxel?
derived_answer: While you're receiving docetaxel treatment, your sense of taste may change and some foods may taste different, such as more salty, bitter, or metallic. You may find that you no longer enjoy foods you used to like. If this happens, speak to your treatment team as they may be able to suggest ways to help manage these taste changes. The good news is that your normal taste should return once your docetaxel treatment has finished. In the meantime, your healthcare team can provide advice and support to help you through this temporary side effect.

question: How can I manage diarrhea or constipation caused by docetaxel?

question: When should I contact my treatment team if I have diarrhea from docetaxel?
derived_answer: You should contact your treatment team if you experience diarrhea 4 or more times within a 24-hour period while taking docetaxel. Frequent diarrhea can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, so it's important to let your healthcare providers know right away if you have 4 or more loose or watery stools in a day. They can then assess your situation, provide medications to help control the diarrhea, and give you guidance on managing your fluid and dietary intake until the diarrhea subsides.

question: What is cancer-related fatigue and how can it be managed during docetaxel treatment?
derived_answer: Cancer-related fatigue is an extreme tiredness that does not go away with rest or sleep. It is a very common side effect of breast cancer treatment like docetaxel, and can affect you both physically and emotionally. If you think you are experiencing this type of fatigue, be sure to tell your GP or treatment team. They can properly assess your fatigue levels and offer advice on managing your energy levels during treatment. There are ways to cope with cancer-related fatigue, so don't hesitate to bring it up with your healthcare providers. They can suggest strategies to help you conserve your energy and get you additional support resources on coping with this exhausting side effect.

question: What should I do if I experience pain, stinging or burning around the IV during chemotherapy?
derived_answer: If you experience any pain, stinging, or a burning sensation around the area where the IV cannula (small plastic tube) is inserted into your vein during your chemotherapy infusion, you should tell your chemotherapy nurse immediately. This could be a sign that the chemotherapy drug is leaking out of the vein, which is called extravasation. If the drug leaks into the surrounding tissue, it can cause damage. By alerting your nurse right away, they can take steps to prevent or minimize any tissue injury.
citation_only: Tell your chemotherapy nurse immediately if you have pain, stinging or a burning sensation around the cannula while the drug is being given.

derived_answer: At the site where the IV cannula is inserted into your vein, you may experience some reactions during or after your docetaxel chemotherapy treatment. While these reactions can be uncomfortable, they are not uncommon side effects and should fade over time as your body heals.

question: Can docetaxel chemotherapy cause lung problems? If so, what are they called?
derived_answer: Yes, docetaxel chemotherapy can potentially cause lung issues as a side effect. It may lead to scarring or inflammation of the lung tissue. This lung condition caused by docetaxel is called interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis. While not one of the most common side effects, your medical team will still monitor you for any lung problems during your treatment. Be sure to report any new or worsening breathing issues right away.

question: What symptoms should I contact my treatment team about immediately?
derived_answer: It's important to contact your treatment team straight away if you experience any of the following symptoms: shortness of breath, a cough (with or without a high temperature), or any new or worsening breathing problems such as chest tightness or wheezing. These could be signs of inflammation in your lungs (interstitial lung disease or ILD), which is a potential side effect of docetaxel treatment. By reporting these symptoms promptly, your medical team can evaluate if you need further testing like a chest X-ray or CT scan to check for ILD. Early treatment of any lung inflammation is crucial to prevent long-term lung damage.

question: What will happen if docetaxel causes inflammation in my lungs?
derived_answer: If docetaxel treatment causes inflammation in your lungs (interstitial lung disease or ILD), your medical team may need to temporarily stop your docetaxel treatment and give you steroids to treat the inflammation. Addressing the lung inflammation early can help prevent long-term damage to your lungs. In some cases, lung damage from ILD can be permanent and may worsen over time. However, treatment for ILD can help relieve symptoms, improve your quality of life, and slow the progression of the disease.

question: What is ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)?
derived_answer: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is an early form of breast cancer. It occurs when abnormal cells start growing inside the milk ducts of the breast, but have not yet spread outside the ducts into the surrounding breast tissue or other parts of the body. DCIS is considered a pre-invasive or non-invasive breast cancer because the cancerous cells are still contained within the ducts. While DCIS needs to be treated, it has a very good prognosis or outlook compared to invasive breast cancers.

question: How does breast cancer start and progress?
derived_answer: Breast cancer starts when cells in the breast begin to divide and grow in an abnormal, uncontrolled way. The breast is made up of milk-producing glands called lobules, and ducts that carry milk to the nipple. These structures are surrounded by tissue that gives the breast its size and shape. In ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), the cancer cells have developed within the milk ducts but have not yet spread outside the ducts into the surrounding breast tissue or other parts of the body. If the cancer cells eventually break out of the ducts and invade the surrounding tissue, it would progress to become invasive breast cancer.

When cancer cells have developed in the ducts and stay in the ducts (in situ), it's called DCIS.

question: What are the typical symptoms of DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ)?
derived_answer: DCIS, or ductal carcinoma in situ, usually does not cause any noticeable symptoms. Most cases of DCIS are found during routine breast cancer screening mammograms or mammograms done for other reasons. However, in some cases, DCIS may be detected if you notice a breast change like a lump or nipple discharge. It's important to be aware that if DCIS is found after noticing a breast change, there is a higher likelihood that invasive breast cancer may also be present. Rarely, some people with DCIS may also develop a rash around the nipple called Paget's disease of the breast. If you notice any breast changes, it's advisable to get them checked by your doctor.

question: How is DCIS diagnosed?
derived_answer: DCIS is diagnosed using a combination of tests and procedures. These may include a mammogram (breast x-ray), an ultrasound scan (which uses sound waves to create an image of the breast), a core biopsy of the breast and sometimes lymph nodes (where a hollow needle is used to take a small tissue sample for examination under a microscope), and a vacuum assisted biopsy (where a special needle connected to a vacuum is used to take a breast tissue sample under local anesthesia for microscopic examination). Your doctor may order one or more of these tests to accurately diagnose DCIS and determine the best course of treatment.

question: What happens during an image-guided biopsy for breast calcifications?
derived_answer: During an image-guided biopsy for breast calcifications, a mammogram or ultrasound is used to precisely locate the area of calcifications in the breast. A small tissue sample is then taken from that area for further examination. The biopsy samples will be x-rayed first to confirm that they contain the calcifications of interest. After that, the samples are sent to a laboratory where they are examined under a microscope by a pathologist to determine if the calcifications are benign or associated with a condition like ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). The image-guided biopsy is an outpatient procedure, so you will be able to leave the clinic soon after it is completed.

Intermediate grade - The cancer cells look less like normal cells and are growing faster than low grade.  High grade - The cancer cells look very different from normal cells and may be fast growing.  The grade can help guide treatment decisions, as higher grade DCIS may be more likely to eventually become invasive breast cancer if left untreated. However, it's important to discuss your specific case and options with your medical team.

question: Can DCIS develop into invasive breast cancer if left untreated?
derived_answer: Yes, if DCIS is not treated, there is a risk that the cancer cells may develop the ability to spread outside the milk ducts into the surrounding breast tissue. This would then be considered invasive breast cancer, which has the potential to metastasize or spread to other parts of the body.  However, it's important to note that in some cases, DCIS may never progress further or may grow so slowly that it would not cause harm during a person's lifetime. Unfortunately, there is currently no way to definitively predict whether an individual case of DCIS will become invasive or not.

question: What is the wire localization procedure like?
derived_answer: For wire localization, a fine wire is inserted into the breast under local anesthetic (medication to numb the area), using a mammogram or ultrasound scan as a guide. You may have the wire inserted on the same day as the DCIS removal surgery, or as an outpatient the day before surgery. The wire will be removed during the surgery to remove the DCIS.

question: What is the purpose of a sentinel lymph node biopsy?
derived_answer: A sentinel lymph node biopsy is performed to check if cancer cells have spread from the breast to the nearby lymph nodes. The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node that cancer cells are likely to spread to from the original tumor site. By removing and examining this lymph node, doctors can determine if the cancer has metastasized beyond the breast. If the sentinel node is clear of cancer cells, it is likely that the other lymph nodes are also clear and do not need to be removed. However, if cancer cells are found in the sentinel node, it may indicate the presence of invasive breast cancer in addition to DCIS, and further treatment may be required.

If the results show the sentinel lymph node is clear of cancer cells, the other nodes are usually clear too, and no more will need to be removed. If the results show the first node or nodes contain cancer cells, this may mean you have an invasive breast cancer as well as DCIS.

question: What is hormone (endocrine) therapy and how does it work for DCIS?
derived_answer: Some breast cancers, including DCIS, use the hormone oestrogen in the body to help them grow. These are known as oestrogen receptor positive or ER-positive. Hormone (endocrine) therapies work by blocking or stopping the effect of oestrogen on breast cancer cells. Different hormone therapy drugs achieve this in different ways. For DCIS that is ER-positive, hormone therapy may be used to reduce the risk of the DCIS coming back or developing into an invasive cancer.

question: What is the purpose of hormone therapy for DCIS?
derived_answer: Hormone therapy can be beneficial for some patients with DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ), which is a non-invasive form of breast cancer. However, hormone therapy is not recommended for everyone with DCIS. Your treatment team will discuss with you the potential benefits, risks, and possible side effects to determine if hormone therapy is appropriate for your specific situation.

question: What happens after I finish my breast cancer treatment at the hospital?

question: What support is available for someone diagnosed with DCIS?

You can also call the Breast Cancer Now helpline at 0808 800 6000 or join their online forum at forum.breastcancernow.org to connect with others going through a similar situation. Don't hesitate to ask for help - letting your family and friends know how you feel can allow them to be more supportive as well.

question: What is breast cancer?
derived_answer: Breast cancer starts when cells in the breast begin to divide and grow in an abnormal and uncontrolled way. Primary breast cancer refers to breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast or the lymph nodes (glands) under the arm. The breasts are made up of lobules (milk-producing glands) and ducts (tubes that carry milk to the nipple), surrounded by tissue that gives the breasts their shape and size. The breasts also contain a network of thin tubes called lymph vessels that are connected to the lymph nodes under the arm.

question: What are the different types of breast cancer?
derived_answer: There are several different types of breast cancer. Breast cancer can be non-invasive (also called 'in situ') or invasive. Most breast cancers are invasive, which means they have the potential to spread to other parts of the body, although this doesn't necessarily mean the cancer has or will spread. Non-invasive breast cancer has not yet developed the ability to spread within the breast or to other parts of the body. The type of breast cancer someone has will determine the appropriate treatment approach for their situation.

question: What is the main goal of treatment for invasive breast cancer?
derived_answer: The main goal of treatment for invasive breast cancer is to remove all the cancer in the breast and any affected lymph nodes under the arm. This is called achieving local control. Treatments like surgery and radiotherapy are used to achieve local control by directly treating the breast area. Additionally, systemic treatments like chemotherapy, hormone therapy, and targeted therapy aim to destroy any cancer cells that may have spread from the breast to other parts of the body through the bloodstream or lymphatic system. These systemic treatments help reduce the risk of the cancer affecting other areas in the future.

question: When is chemotherapy given for breast cancer?

Chemotherapy usually starts a few weeks after surgery to allow your body time to recover. Chemotherapy can also be given before surgery, which is called primary or neo-adjuvant chemotherapy. The aim is to slow the growth of the cancer or shrink a larger breast cancer before surgery, potentially allowing for breast-conserving surgery instead of a mastectomy. In some cases, chemotherapy may be given both before and after surgery.

question: What is trastuzumab and how does it work?
derived_answer: Trastuzumab is a targeted (biological) therapy used in the treatment of breast cancer. It works by blocking the growth and spread of cancer cells. Targeted therapies like trastuzumab interfere with specific processes in the cells that help cancer grow. Trastuzumab targets and disrupts these processes, preventing the cancer from continuing to grow and spread.

question: How does the drug trastuzumab work to treat breast cancer?
derived_answer: Trastuzumab is a targeted therapy that works specifically for HER2 positive breast cancers. Some breast cancer cells have higher than normal levels of a protein called HER2 on their surface, which helps the cancer cells grow. Trastuzumab attaches to these HER2 proteins, preventing the cancer cells from receiving growth signals. It also helps the body's immune system recognize and destroy the HER2 positive breast cancer cells. By targeting the HER2 proteins, trastuzumab can effectively treat HER2 positive breast cancers.
citation_only: Trastuzumab works by attaching itself to the HER2 proteins so that the cancer cells are no longer stimulated to grow. It also helps the body's immune system destroy breast cancer cells.

question: Who can benefit from taking trastuzumab for breast cancer treatment?

If your breast cancer is HER2 negative, meaning it does not have higher than normal levels of the HER2 protein, then trastuzumab will not be an effective treatment option for you. Your doctor will perform tests on a sample of your breast tissue to determine the HER2 status before recommending trastuzumab.

If you have heart problems, you may be referred to a cardiologist (heart specialist) for further evaluation to determine if trastuzumab is safe for you. Your doctor wants to ensure your heart is healthy enough to tolerate this breast cancer therapy.

question: How do doctors determine if my breast cancer is HER2 positive or HER2 negative?
derived_answer: All invasive breast cancers are tested for HER2 levels to determine if they are HER2 positive or negative. This testing is done in a hospital laboratory on a sample of your breast cancer tissue that was removed during a biopsy or surgery. The results usually take 1 to 3 weeks to come back. The first test done is called an IHC (immunohistochemistry) test, which involves staining the tissue sample. This test gives a score from 0 to 3+, with 0 or 1+ meaning HER2 negative, 2+ being borderline, and 3+ indicating HER2 positive. If the result is borderline at 2+, more specialized tests are done to definitively determine if your cancer is HER2 positive, HER2 low, or HER2 negative. Knowing your HER2 status helps guide the best treatment options for your particular breast cancer.

These tests give a result of HER2 positive, HER2 low or HER2 negative.

question: What does it mean if my breast cancer is HER2 low?
derived_answer: If your breast cancer tests show it is HER2 low, this means the levels of the HER2 protein are not high enough to be considered HER2 positive, but are higher than HER2 negative cancers. There is some emerging evidence that HER2 low breast cancers may potentially benefit from targeted treatments like trastuzumab (Herceptin), which targets the HER2 protein. However, more research is still needed in this area. As of now, targeted HER2 treatment for HER2 low breast cancers is not yet available outside of clinical trials. If your results show HER2 low status, I'd recommend discussing this with your oncology team to understand if any clinical trials or new treatment options may be appropriate for your specific situation.

question: What should I do if my breast cancer tests show a borderline HER2 result?
derived_answer: If your initial HER2 testing comes back as borderline or a 2+ score, don't worry - this doesn't mean the results are inconclusive. In this situation, more specialized tests will be done to definitively determine if your breast cancer is HER2 positive, HER2 low, or HER2 negative. These additional tests are more in-depth and provide a clear result about your HER2 status. The borderline 2+ score just means further evaluation is needed. Your care team will order the appropriate follow-up testing and go over the final results with you once they come back. Getting an accurate HER2 classification is important for guiding the best treatment approach for your specific type of breast cancer.

question: When is trastuzumab given for primary breast cancer?
derived_answer: Trastuzumab can be given for primary breast cancer (breast cancer that has not spread beyond the breast or lymph nodes under the arm) in two main situations:  Before surgery (neo-adjuvant or primary therapy): Trastuzumab may be given before surgery, along with chemotherapy and often pertuzumab, to slow down the cancer's growth and reduce the chance of it spreading. It can also help shrink a large breast cancer before surgery.  After surgery (adjuvant treatment): Trastuzumab can be given after surgery to reduce the risk of the breast cancer returning or spreading to other parts of the body. It may be given with or after chemotherapy, and sometimes with pertuzumab as well.  If you received trastuzumab before surgery, it will usually continue for around 6 to 12 months after surgery. Your treatment team can explain the specific reasons and timing for recommending trastuzumab in your situation.

question: What types of breast cancer can trastuzumab be used to treat?
derived_answer: Trastuzumab may be used to treat people who have: • Local recurrence – breast cancer that has come back in the chest/breast area or in the skin near the original site or scar • Locally advanced breast – breast cancer that has spread to the tissues and lymph nodes (glands) around the chest, neck and under the breastbone (when surgery is not possible) • Secondary (metastatic) breast cancer – breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body

Don't hesitate to ask them any questions you may have about how you will receive this medication.

derived_answer: The first intravenous infusion of trastuzumab is called a loading dose, and it is typically given over an hour and a half. After receiving this initial dose, you may be asked to remain at the hospital for several hours to ensure you are feeling well before leaving. This allows the healthcare team to monitor you for any potential side effects or reactions.

For subsequent doses, you may not need to stay as long if there are no issues with the first injection.

question: How long will I receive trastuzumab treatment?
derived_answer: The duration of your trastuzumab treatment depends on the specific type and stage of your breast cancer. If you are receiving trastuzumab to treat primary breast cancer after surgery, it is usually given for 1 year (around 18 cycles), although some people may be offered a 6-month course. If you are receiving trastuzumab before surgery, you will typically have 4 to 6 cycles, and you may also receive additional trastuzumab for up to 1 year after surgery. For secondary (metastatic) breast cancer, trastuzumab is usually given for as long as it continues to effectively control the cancer.

question: What are some common side effects of trastuzumab?
derived_answer: Trastuzumab, like any treatment, can cause side effects. Some common side effects include flu-like symptoms such as fever, chills, and mild pain in some parts of the body, especially after the first dose. These symptoms usually don't last long. Extreme fatigue or tiredness that doesn't go away with rest is also a very common side effect. The fatigue can last for weeks or months after treatment ends, and in some cases, it can be a long-term effect. It's important to let your treatment team know if you experience fatigue so they can rule out other conditions like anemia. There are ways to cope with and manage fatigue, and your team can help you with this.
citation_only:
Common side effects 
Flu-like symptoms
Fever, chills and mild pain in some parts of the body can occur during or shortly after your treatment. These symptoms are more common the first time you have trastuzumab and do not usually last long. Taking pain relief can help. 
Extreme tiredness 
Fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that does not go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally. 
It's a very common side effect of trastuzumab and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect. 
Fatigue can also be caused by conditions such as anaemia (too few red blood cells). It's important to let your team know if you're affected by fatigue to rule out other conditions.

Fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that does not go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally. 
It's a very common side effect of trastuzumab and may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished. Occasionally fatigue is a long-term effect. 
Fatigue can also be caused by conditions such as anaemia (too few red blood cells). It's important to let your team know if you're affected by fatigue to rule out other conditions.

Your heart function will be closely monitored with tests like echocardiograms or MUGA scans before starting treatment, regularly during treatment, and potentially for 2 years after your last dose. Heart problems are more likely if trastuzumab is given along with chemotherapy or if you already have a heart condition.

question: What is a pulmonary embolism, and how is it related to blood clots?
derived_answer: A pulmonary embolism (PE) is a serious condition that can occur when part of a blood clot breaks away and travels to the lung. People with a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which is a type of blood clot, are at risk of developing a pulmonary embolism. This happens when a piece of the blood clot dislodges and travels through the bloodstream, potentially blocking an artery in the lung. Pulmonary embolisms can be life-threatening, so it's crucial to seek immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood.

question: Is it safe to take trastuzumab during pregnancy?

If you think you may be pregnant while on trastuzumab treatment, it's important to stop the medication and inform your specialist right away. Your doctor will advise you on the best course of action to ensure the safety of you and your baby.

It's important to use effective contraception during treatment and for 7 months after finishing trastuzumab.

You may feel very low at times, followed by periods of feeling more positive. Some people also experience physical symptoms like loss of appetite, diarrhea, or difficulty sleeping. The days and weeks immediately following the diagnosis can be particularly emotional and challenging. It's important to be gentle with yourself and allow yourself to process the news in your own way.

question: What are some common ways to deal with stress and anxiety after a breast cancer diagnosis?
derived_answer: It's very common to feel stressed and anxious after receiving a breast cancer diagnosis. This can be a new experience for some, or it may worsen existing anxiety. There are several healthy ways to reduce stress and anxiety, such as distraction through hobbies or interests, relaxation techniques like visualization or meditation, regular exercise, counseling to explore your feelings, or cognitive behavioral therapy to change unhelpful thought patterns. Your breast care nurse or doctor can advise you on accessing these supportive techniques. It's important to find positive coping methods rather than turning to unhealthy habits during this difficult time.
citation_only: There are many ways to reduce stress and anxiety, including: • Distraction – focusing on things around you, or a hobby or interest, to shut out negative thoughts • Relaxation, visualisation, mindfulness and meditation – you can use these separately or together to reduce stress and tension • Exercise – regular physical activity, whether it's a brisk walk or yoga, can help clear your mind and reduce your stress levels • One-to-one counselling – explore feelings which can be related to your cancer diagnosis, making them easier to understand and cope with • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) – can help you to change patterns of thinking and behaviour that may be stopping you from moving forward

question: How can I tell my family and friends about my breast cancer diagnosis?
derived_answer: Telling your family and friends about your breast cancer diagnosis can be very difficult. It's a personal decision who you want to tell and how you want to share the news. You may want to start by sharing the basic facts about your diagnosis and treatment options, and let the conversation progress naturally from there. Some people find it helpful to tell a few close friends or family members first, and ask them to help spread the word to others. If you use social media or messaging apps, you could consider creating a private group to share the news, so you don't have to repeat yourself multiple times. Just be clear about who you want to know at this point. It's understandable to worry about how your loved ones will react - some may be upset, some uncomfortable, and others may struggle to process the news initially. Don't be surprised if some people seem to avoid mentioning your cancer, as they may simply be worried about upsetting you. It can help to openly discuss your feelings with your close friends and family, and let them know how they can best support you during this time.

question: How should I tell my children that I have breast cancer?
derived_answer: Telling children that you have breast cancer can feel very daunting, but it's best to be open with them sooner rather than later. Children are perceptive and can often sense when something is wrong, which may cause them to worry or make guesses about what's happening. The best approach is to keep the explanation simple and avoid complicated details. Their understanding and reaction will depend on their age and personality. It's important to be honest with children in an age-appropriate way, as evidence suggests they are less frightened when they know what is going on, even if they don't fully understand. You can find more guidance on how to have this conversation in the 'Talking with children about primary breast cancer' booklet or on the Breast Cancer Now website.

question: Do I have to tell my employer about my breast cancer diagnosis and treatment?
derived_answer: No, you don't have to tell your employer about your breast cancer diagnosis and treatment if you don't want to. However, your employer does have a duty to make reasonable adjustments to your role or working environment to help you do your job. If you don't inform them about your diagnosis and treatment, it may be difficult for them to know what adjustments to make for you. You cannot lose your job or be treated less favorably for having breast cancer. Any information you provide to your employer about your condition must be kept private and only discussed with others with your permission.

question: What are clinical trials and what do they involve?
derived_answer: Clinical trials are research studies involving people that aim to improve various aspects of cancer diagnosis, treatment, and care. They are voluntary and may involve looking at ways to reduce cancer risk, improve screening and diagnosis methods, test new drugs or treatments, find better ways to combine treatments, reduce side effects, assess quality of life impacts, or evaluate supportive care approaches like psychological support. Clinical trials play an important role in advancing medical knowledge and improving patient outcomes.

question: What is invasive lobular breast cancer?
derived_answer: Invasive lobular breast cancer is a type of breast cancer that starts in the lobules, which are the milk-producing glands of the breast. The term 'invasive' means that the cancer cells have spread from the lobules into the surrounding breast tissue. It may also be called invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast or ILC. While invasive lobular breast cancer can affect women of any age, it is more common as women get older. It is very rare in men.

"Invasive" means the cancer cells have spread outside the lobules into the surrounding breast tissue. You may also hear it called invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast or ILC.

question: What are some common symptoms of invasive lobular breast cancer?
derived_answer: Some common symptoms of invasive lobular breast cancer include a thickening of the breast tissue, a change in the shape or size of the breast, changes in skin texture like puckering or dimpling, a lump or swelling under the arm, changes to the nipple, and discharge from the nipple. However, it's important to note that invasive lobular breast cancer may not always cause obvious changes to the breast. You may be diagnosed through routine breast screening before noticing any symptoms yourself.

question: What types of surgery are typically used to treat invasive lobular breast cancer?
derived_answer: The first treatment for invasive lobular breast cancer is usually surgery. The two main types of surgery are breast-conserving surgery (removal of the cancer with a margin of normal breast tissue around it, also called wide local excision or lumpectomy) and mastectomy (removal of all the breast tissue, usually including the nipple area). The type of surgery recommended will depend on factors like where the cancer is located in the breast, the size of the cancer in relation to the breast size, and whether more than one area in the breast is affected. You can discuss your options with your treatment team to decide what is best for your specific situation.

derived_answer: A sentinel lymph node biopsy is a procedure where the first lymph node(s) that cancer cells are likely to spread to are removed and checked for cancer. This helps determine if the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes under the arm. The results help guide whether additional treatment after surgery may be beneficial. The sentinel node biopsy is usually done at the same time as the breast cancer surgery, but can also be done beforehand.

There may be more than one sentinel lymph node. The procedure is usually done at the same time as your cancer surgery but may be done before. If the results show the sentinel lymph node is clear of cancer cells, the other nodes are usually clear too, and no more will need to be removed.

Details on prosthesis options are covered in the 'Breast prostheses, bras and clothes after surgery' booklet.  3. Choosing not to have reconstruction or wear a prosthesis after the mastectomy.

question: What is chemotherapy and how does it work for breast cancer?
derived_answer: Chemotherapy is a treatment that destroys cancer cells by affecting their ability to divide and grow. question: What is hormone therapy and how does it work for breast cancer?
derived_answer: Hormone therapy is a type of treatment used for breast cancers that are estrogen receptor positive (ER-positive). These cancers use the hormone estrogen in the body to help them grow. Different hormone therapy drugs achieve this in different ways, such as blocking estrogen receptors or reducing estrogen production. Hormone therapy is only prescribed if your breast cancer tests positive for estrogen receptors.

It does this by inhibiting an enzyme called aromatase that is involved in producing estrogen in the body after menopause.

question: What is cancer-related fatigue and how can I manage it while taking exemestane?
derived_answer: Cancer-related fatigue is extreme tiredness and exhaustion that doesn't go away with rest or sleep. It can affect you physically and emotionally, and is a very common side effect of taking exemestane. The fatigue may last for weeks or months after your treatment has finished, and occasionally it can be a long-term effect. It's important to let your GP or treatment team know if you're experiencing fatigue so they can rule out other conditions like anemia. There are various ways to cope with and manage fatigue, such as getting enough rest, staying active, and trying relaxation techniques. You can find more information and tips for managing fatigue on the Breast Cancer Now website or by calling their Helpline.

question: What types of treatments can cause hair loss in breast cancer patients?
derived_answer: Chemotherapy is a common treatment for breast cancer that can lead to hair loss. Chemotherapy works by interfering with the ability of cancer cells to divide and grow, but it can also affect healthy cells like those in the hair follicles. This is why chemotherapy can cause hair loss on the head, as well as loss of body hair like eyebrows, eyelashes, nasal hair, pubic hair, and chest hair in men. Not all chemotherapy drugs will make your hair fall out completely - some may just cause thinning. The likelihood and extent of hair loss depends on the specific drugs used, the dosage, and whether you receive a combination of chemotherapy drugs. Your treatment team will discuss with you how likely you are to experience hair loss based on your particular chemotherapy regimen.

As well as the hair on your head, this can also affect your body hair including eyebrows, eyelashes, nasal and pubic hair, and chest hair for men (see page 37). Not all chemotherapy will make your hair fall out. Some drugs don't cause any hair loss and some will cause hair to thin. However, others make hair fall out completely. The most commonly used chemotherapy drugs to treat breast cancer will cause some hair loss.

question: How does the dosage and frequency of chemotherapy affect hair loss?
derived_answer: The extent of hair loss experienced during chemotherapy can depend on the specific dosage and frequency of the drugs given. Chemotherapy drugs that are administered in smaller, more frequent doses on a weekly basis or taken orally are less likely to cause complete hair loss compared to higher doses given every 2-3 weeks. If you receive a combination of multiple chemotherapy drugs, you are also more likely to experience significant hair loss. The timing of when hair loss begins can also vary - with hair typically starting to fall out or thin 2-3 weeks after the first treatment for regimens given every 2-3 weeks, or more gradually for weekly chemotherapy. Your oncology team will discuss your particular chemotherapy plan and the likelihood of hair loss based on the drugs, doses, and schedule.

question: Can radiotherapy cause hair loss?
derived_answer: Yes, radiotherapy can cause hair loss, but only in the specific area being treated. Unlike chemotherapy which can cause full body hair loss, radiotherapy affects healthy cells as well as cancer cells in the targeted area. So you will only lose hair from the part of your body that receives radiation treatment. For example, if you receive radiotherapy to your breast and armpit lymph nodes, you may lose underarm hair and chest hair in the treated areas. Men may also lose chest hair from the radiated part of their chest. If radiotherapy is given to treat brain metastases, you may experience hair loss on your head depending on whether the whole brain or just a targeted area is radiated.
citation_only: Radiotherapy uses high-energy x-rays to destroy cancer cells. Like chemotherapy, it affects healthy cells as well as cancer cells so can cause hair loss, but only in the specific area being treated. This means that you will only lose hair from that area. If you're having radiotherapy to the lymph nodes in your armpit as well as your breast you'll lose underarm hair in the area that has been treated. Men may also lose chest hair from the part of their chest that has been treated.

The likelihood of hair loss may increase if hormone therapy is combined with other treatments like chemotherapy or targeted therapy.

derived_answer: Some people find it helpful to prepare for hair loss before starting cancer treatment. This can give you a sense of control over the hair loss process rather than waiting for it to happen gradually. If you shave your hair, be sure to use clippers with a guard to avoid scratching or cutting your scalp, which could lead to infection. Another option is to donate your hair if you have it cut off, as there are organizations that use donated hair to make wigs for people experiencing hair loss. If you plan to wear a wig, it can be useful to choose and try it on before losing your hair, to help you get used to it and ensure it matches your natural hair color and style.

question: What is scalp cooling and how does it work?
derived_answer: Scalp cooling is a technique that may help prevent hair loss during chemotherapy treatment. It works by reducing the blood flow to the hair follicles, which reduces the amount of chemotherapy drugs that reach them. This is done by wearing a cold cap or using a refrigerated cooling system that continuously pumps a liquid coolant through a cap worn on the head. The cooling helps to constrict the blood vessels in the scalp, limiting the chemotherapy drugs from reaching and damaging the hair follicles. However, scalp cooling does not work for everyone and its effectiveness depends on the specific chemotherapy drugs and doses used.

This is due to the possibility that the constricted blood vessels caused by cooling could limit the amount of chemotherapy drugs reaching the scalp, potentially allowing any cancer cells present to survive and spread. However, the leaflet does not provide definitive information on whether this risk has been conclusively proven or how significant it may be. It's important to discuss the potential risks and benefits of scalp cooling with your oncologist to make an informed decision.

derived_answer: When using a cold cap during chemotherapy, some people may experience discomfort, aching, and sometimes nausea in the first 10-15 minutes of the treatment. question: What tips are recommended for caring for hair during cancer treatment?
derived_answer: Here are some helpful tips for caring for your hair during cancer treatment:  - Use a mild, unperfumed shampoo and conditioner to avoid irritating your scalp. - Try to wash your hair no more than twice a week, but at least once every 10 days. - Use warm water instead of hot water when washing your hair. - Pat your hair dry gently instead of rubbing it vigorously with a towel. - Be gentle when brushing or combing your hair. Use a soft hairbrush or wide-tooth plastic comb. - Massage your scalp gently to improve blood flow to the hair follicles, which can promote hair health.  Following these tips can help minimize hair damage and discomfort during cancer treatment when your hair may be more fragile. Be gentle with your hair and avoid harsh products or styling methods.

question: How can I tie a headscarf or bandana to cover my hair loss?
derived_answer: Here are step-by-step instructions for tying a headscarf or bandana:  1. Lay a square headscarf flat with the underside facing up. Fold the headscarf diagonally into a triangle. 2. Place the headscarf on your head with the folded edge about 2.5cm below your natural hairline and the points at the back.  3. Tie the outer points into a double knot behind your head over the middle triangle point (or a single knot if doing a more complex wrap). 4. The flap should be underneath the knot. Pull any excess headscarf from under the knot.  Following these steps can help you securely and stylishly cover your head with a headscarf or bandana.

derived_answer: There are a few options to help camouflage long-lasting hair loss or thinning hair. However, these systems can be time-consuming and expensive since they are not currently covered by the NHS.

question: Why is it important to do exercises after breast cancer surgery?
derived_answer: Doing exercises after breast cancer surgery is important for several reasons. First, it can help you regain arm and shoulder movement that may have been affected by the surgery and radiotherapy. Muscles and joints can become stiff and immobile very quickly if they are not used, so doing these exercises as part of your daily routine can help prevent this. Additionally, the exercises can improve symptoms caused by tight scars and cording, which is a buildup of scar tissue that can cause blood vessels to become stuck, feeling like a tight cord running down your affected arm. The exercises can also help prevent long-term problems with arm and shoulder movement, posture, and stiffness. Furthermore, they can reduce the risk of lymphoedema, which is swelling of the arm, hand, breast, or chest area caused by a buildup of lymph fluid. It's crucial to do these exercises to aid in your recovery and prevent potential complications.

question: What are some basic exercises I can do after breast cancer surgery?
derived_answer: After breast cancer surgery, you can do some basic exercises while sitting or standing. During the first week, avoid raising your arms above shoulder level (90 degrees). Some recommended exercises include:  Bent arm forwards - Bend your elbows and rest your hands lightly on your shoulders. Raise both arms forward so they are at right angles to your body, then lower your elbows slowly.  Bent arm sideways - Rest your hands on your shoulders, then raise your elbows out to the sides. Lower your elbows slowly.  Back scratching - Hold your arms out to the sides and bend from the elbows. Slowly reach up behind your back to just under your shoulder blades, then lower your arms back down.  Winging it - Place your hands behind your head with elbows pointing forwards. Bring your elbows back so they're pointing out to the sides, then return to the starting position.  These gentle exercises can help improve mobility and flexibility after surgery. Be sure to follow your doctor's guidance on when to start exercises and how far to push yourself.

question: What are some advanced exercises I can do after recovering from breast cancer surgery?
derived_answer: As you recover further from breast cancer surgery, you can try some more advanced exercises like wall climbing. This exercise has two steps:  Step 1: Stand facing a wall with your feet apart. Put both hands on the wall at shoulder level. Looking straight ahead, gradually work your hands up the wall by sliding them or using your fingers to climb as high as you can while feeling a stretch but not pain. Hold at the highest point for 10 seconds, then slide your hands back down to shoulder level before repeating.  Step 2: Stand sideways to the wall with your affected side nearest the wall. Put your hand on the wall with your elbow bent and shoulders relaxed. Look straight ahead and gradually creep your hand up the wall as far as possible, allowing your elbow to straighten. Hold for 10 seconds, then lower your hand back down.  The wall climbing exercise helps improve overhead mobility and flexibility after surgery. Start gently and try to increase your range a little more each time. Listen to your body and don't push too far to avoid pain or discomfort.

question: How do I perform arm lifts after breast cancer surgery?
derived_answer: To perform arm lifts after breast cancer surgery, lie down on your bed or the floor with a pillow supporting your head. Take a few deep breaths and relax your shoulders so they are not hunched up. Clasp your hands together or hold a stick/broom handle with straight elbows. Lift your arms up and over your head as far as comfortable. Hold for 10 seconds, then slowly lower your arms. You can place a pillow behind you to support your arms until you can lift them further back. If you have difficulty lying down, you can do this exercise sitting in a chair, leaning back. If you can't lie completely flat, prop your head and upper back on pillows and reduce the number of pillows as you get more comfortable.

question: What is letrozole?
derived_answer: Letrozole is a hormone therapy drug used to treat breast cancer in women who have gone through menopause (when periods stop). It can also be used in premenopausal women who are receiving treatment to stop their ovaries from working (ovarian suppression). Letrozole is the generic name for the drug, but you may hear it called by its most well-known brand name Femara. There are other brand names that contain the same dose of letrozole.

question: How does letrozole work to treat breast cancer?
derived_answer: Letrozole works by reducing the amount of the hormone estrogen made in the body. Some breast cancers, known as estrogen receptor positive (ER+) breast cancers, use estrogen to help them grow. Letrozole will only be prescribed if your breast cancer is ER+. It reduces estrogen levels by blocking the action of an enzyme called aromatase, which is involved in producing estrogen in the body after menopause.

Before the menopause, oestrogen is mainly produced in the ovaries. After the menopause, the ovaries no longer produce oestrogen, but some oestrogen is still made in body fat. This process involves an enzyme (a type of protein) called aromatase.

question: What is letrozole and how does it work?
derived_answer: Letrozole belongs to a group of drugs called aromatase inhibitors. These drugs work by stopping the aromatase enzyme from functioning, which reduces the amount of estrogen in the body. Estrogen can help breast cancer cells grow, so by lowering estrogen levels, aromatase inhibitors like letrozole can help prevent the growth and spread of certain types of breast cancer.

Letrozole may also be considered for some breast cancers that are only progesterone receptor positive (PR+), though this is less common.

question: When is letrozole prescribed for breast cancer treatment?
derived_answer: Letrozole is typically prescribed for women who have gone through menopause and have estrogen receptor positive breast cancer. It may be given after surgery to reduce the risk of the cancer returning or spreading further in the body, which is known as adjuvant or additional therapy. In some cases, letrozole may be used before surgery to shrink a larger breast tumor, or as the first treatment if surgery is not appropriate initially. Your doctor will discuss the best timing for you to take letrozole as part of your breast cancer treatment plan.

question: How should letrozole be taken?

question: How does letrozole affect bone health?
derived_answer: According to the information provided, letrozole, a medication used in breast cancer treatment, reduces the amount of estrogen in the body. A lack of estrogen over time can lead to osteoporosis, which is a condition characterized by thinning and weakening of the bones. To monitor bone health, the specialist may order a scan to check the strength and thickness (density) of the patient's bones before or shortly after starting letrozole treatment. If the patient has been given bisphosphonates as part of their treatment, a scan may not be necessary. The bone density may be checked every two to three years while the patient is taking letrozole, depending on the initial scan results or if the specialist has any concerns.

question: How does chemotherapy affect fertility and periods in younger women with breast cancer?
derived_answer: Chemotherapy can have a significant impact on fertility and menstrual cycles in younger women with breast cancer. It can temporarily or permanently stop your periods, depending on factors like the specific drugs used, dosage, your age, and your fertility levels before treatment. The likelihood of lasting effects on fertility increases with higher doses of chemotherapy drugs and older age, particularly if you're over 35. If your periods return after chemotherapy, it's still likely that you'll go through menopause earlier than expected. Even if your periods come back, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll be able to get pregnant. It's important to discuss any concerns about fertility with your treatment team.

question: What is osteoporosis and how can breast cancer treatment increase the risk of developing it?
derived_answer: Osteoporosis is a condition where the bones lose strength and density, making them more prone to fractures. Certain breast cancer treatments can increase the risk of developing osteoporosis. An early menopause before age 45 leads to lower estrogen levels, which is a risk factor. Some hormone therapy drugs used to treat breast cancer can also lower estrogen and increase osteoporosis risk. It's important to discuss your individual risk with your treatment team.

question: What legal protections do people with breast cancer have in the workplace?
derived_answer: In the UK, people with breast cancer are protected from discrimination at work under the Equality Act 2010. The Act classifies anyone who has or has had cancer as disabled, which safeguards them from unfair treatment in the workplace, including during the hiring process. Your employer is legally required to make reasonable adjustments to accommodate your needs and enable you to continue working or return to work after treatment. This could involve a gradual return to work, temporary changes to your hours or workload, time off for medical appointments, or adjustments to your role and responsibilities.

question: What happens after I finish my breast cancer treatment at the hospital?
derived_answer: After you complete your hospital treatment for breast cancer, you will continue to be monitored through follow-up care. question: How often will I get mammograms during my follow-up after breast cancer treatment?
derived_answer: After completing breast cancer treatment, you will typically have follow-up mammograms scheduled annually for at least the first 5 years. The mammograms allow your doctors to monitor for any signs that the cancer may have returned. Depending on your age, you may continue to have annual mammograms for longer than 5 years. Once you reach around age 50, you will be invited to participate in the national breast screening program for routine mammograms. The specifics of your mammogram schedule will depend on the type of surgery you had - if you had breast-conserving surgery, both breasts will be imaged. If you had a mastectomy, only the remaining breast will be imaged annually. No mammograms are needed if you had a double mastectomy removing both breasts.
citation_only: You'll have a follow-up mammogram every year for at least 5 years. However, you may have these for longer depending on your age. At around the age of 50, you'll be invited to take part in a national breast screening programme. If you had breast-conserving surgery, you'll have a mammogram on both breasts. If you had a mastectomy (with or without reconstruction), you'll have a mammogram on your other breast. If you had a double (bilateral) mastectomy, you will not have mammograms.

question: What is breast reconstruction?
derived_answer: Breast reconstruction is a surgical procedure to create a new breast shape after breast cancer surgery. It can be done after a mastectomy (removal of the whole breast) or breast-conserving surgery (removal of part of the breast). The new breast shape is created using either a breast implant, your own tissue from another part of the body, or a combination of both. Your treatment team will explain the benefits and limitations of the different reconstruction options suitable for you.
citation_only: Breast reconstruction is surgery to create a new breast shape. It may be done after surgery to remove your whole breast (mastectomy) or part of the breast (breast-conserving surgery).

question: When can breast reconstruction be done?
derived_answer: Breast reconstruction can be done at different times in relation to your breast cancer surgery. It can be done immediately at the same time as a mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery. Alternatively, it can be delayed and done months or years later after the initial surgery. Some patients may also be offered a two-stage approach called a delayed-immediate reconstruction.

question: What are the different types of breast reconstruction?
derived_answer: There are a few different ways a new breast shape can be created during breast reconstruction surgery. The options include using a breast implant, using your own tissue from another part of your body (such as the abdomen or back), or a combination of an implant and your own tissue. question: What is the main goal of breast reconstruction surgery?
derived_answer: The primary aim of breast reconstruction surgery is to create a new breast shape that looks as natural as possible and matches the size, shape, and position of the remaining breast. The goal is to achieve symmetry and proportion between the reconstructed breast and the other breast, so that they appear balanced and in harmony with your body shape. While there may be some differences between the reconstructed breast and the natural breast, the surgery aims to provide the most cosmetically pleasing and natural-looking outcome.

This allows your body to heal fully from those treatments first.  - You'll have more time to consider your options and make a decision about the specific type of reconstruction you would like, without feeling rushed into a choice.  - If you have any pre-existing medical conditions, delaying the reconstruction allows time for those to be managed properly so the surgery can be done as safely as possible.  The main benefit is being able to complete cancer treatments first and make a fully informed decision, though you will have to go flat-chested for a period before the delayed reconstruction.

question: What are some potential downsides or limitations of delayed breast reconstruction?
derived_answer: Some potential downsides or limitations of having delayed breast reconstruction include:  - You will be flat on that side after your mastectomy and may want to wear an external breast prosthesis for symmetry until you have the delayed reconstruction surgery, which could be many months or years later.  - The cosmetic appearance and results may not be as good as if you had an immediate reconstruction done at the same time as the mastectomy.  - There may be more overall scarring with a delayed reconstruction compared to immediate.  - You will not be able to keep your nipple area with a delayed procedure.  - If you had radiation therapy before the delayed reconstruction, it may limit your options for the type of reconstruction you can have.  - While delayed reconstruction is available through the NHS, in some areas there may be long wait times before you can get scheduled for the surgery.

question: What are some important questions to ask my surgeon before deciding on breast reconstruction?
derived_answer: It's important to discuss your breast reconstruction surgery thoroughly with your surgeon beforehand to ensure you fully understand the process and have realistic expectations. Some key questions to ask include: Which type of reconstruction would be best for your specific situation and why? What are the benefits, limitations, and risks of that surgical approach? Are you a suitable candidate for immediate reconstruction at the same time as your mastectomy? It's also wise to ask how the reconstruction may impact the timing of other treatments like chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Additionally, you'll want to understand the surgical details, such as where the scars will be located, whether nipple preservation is possible, and what options exist for nipple recreation later on. Writing down your questions beforehand and bringing someone with you can help ensure all your concerns are addressed.

question: What is breast-conserving surgery and how does it differ from a full mastectomy?
derived_answer: Breast-conserving surgery, also known as a lumpectomy or wide local excision, is a surgical procedure where only the cancerous tumor and a small margin of surrounding breast tissue are removed, rather than the entire breast. Unlike a full mastectomy which removes the whole breast, breast-conserving surgery aims to preserve as much of the healthy breast tissue as possible. This can be a good option for some women with early-stage breast cancer, allowing them to keep most of their breast intact.

question: If I have breast-conserving surgery, will I need breast reconstruction?

The goal of breast-conserving surgery is to remove the cancerous area while preserving as much of the natural breast shape and appearance as possible. However, in some cases, surgical techniques like oncoplastic surgery may be used during the lumpectomy to help reshape and maintain the symmetry of the breast after tumor removal.

question: What is oncoplastic surgery and how can it help after breast-conserving surgery?
derived_answer: Oncoplastic surgery refers to combining the surgical removal of the cancer with plastic surgery techniques to improve the cosmetic appearance and shape of the breast. After a lumpectomy or breast-conserving surgery, oncoplastic techniques can be used to reposition the remaining breast tissue to fill in the area where the tumor was removed and reshape the breast. This helps maintain symmetry and a natural look to the breast.

question: How is the remaining breast tissue repositioned after a lumpectomy?
derived_answer: During the same operation to remove the cancerous tumor through a lumpectomy, the remaining healthy breast tissue can be surgically repositioned and reshaped to fill in the area where the cancer was removed. This technique is known as therapeutic mammoplasty. It allows the surgeon to reconstruct the breast's shape and appearance using the patient's own tissue after the lumpectomy.

question: What is partial breast reconstruction and what procedures are involved?
derived_answer: Partial breast reconstruction is a procedure that involves replacing breast tissue that has been removed due to cancer treatment. It uses skin and fat from the side of the chest or the back. Some specific procedures include LICAP (lateral intercostal artery perforator) flap, LTAP (lateral thoracic artery perforator) flap, AICAP (anterior intercostal artery perforator) flap, and MICAP (medial intercostal artery perforator) flap. These procedures take their names from the blood vessels in the areas of the body where the tissue is taken from. Partial breast reconstruction can be used when cancer has been removed from the outer or lower part of the breast.

derived_answer: Breast reconstruction using an implant involves using a breast implant to restore the shape and volume of the breast after a mastectomy. This type of reconstruction can be done immediately after the mastectomy or at a later time (delayed reconstruction).

derived_answer: Having breast reconstruction with an implant can offer several benefits. question: What are the limitations of breast reconstruction with implants?
derived_answer: There are several potential limitations to consider with breast reconstruction using implants. The implants may feel firmer, colder, and move less naturally compared to reconstruction using your own tissue. When not wearing a bra, there may be a more obvious difference in shape between the reconstructed breast and natural breast, as the reconstructed one is less likely to droop. You will have scars on or around the reconstructed breast. The reconstructed breast will also have less or no sensation compared to the natural breast. You may need future surgeries to replace a damaged implant, address hardening around the implant, or create a better match with the other breast. If you have an expander implant, you may need more hospital visits to expand it. Some people notice folds or wrinkles on the skin at the top of the implant, known as rippling.

question: When might a tissue expander implant be recommended over a fixed-volume implant?
derived_answer: A tissue expander implant may be recommended over a fixed-volume implant in a few situations:  1. If you do not have enough skin left on your chest after mastectomy to comfortably cover and support a fixed-volume implant, especially if you are having delayed breast reconstruction surgery. The expander allows the skin to slowly stretch.  2. If you have had a skin-sparing mastectomy and your treatment team is concerned about wound healing issues. The gradual expansion may be better tolerated.  3. If you have had radiotherapy, as this reduces the elasticity and quality of the skin. Tissue expanders may not be suitable after radiotherapy for this reason.

question: How do tissue expander implants compare to fixed-volume silicone implants in terms of look and feel?
derived_answer: Tissue expander implants can sometimes feel heavier, firmer and less natural in look and feel compared to fixed-volume silicone gel implants. The silicone gel implants tend to have a more natural, soft feel and appearance once the reconstruction has fully healed.  While tissue expanders allow the skin to stretch gradually, the expansion process and saline filling can result in a firmer, heavier feeling implant compared to the cohesive silicone gel used in fixed-volume implants. The silicone gel more closely mimics the look and feel of natural breast tissue.

question: What are the different types of implant reconstruction for breast cancer?
derived_answer: There are a few different options for implant reconstruction after breast cancer surgery. One is called immediate reconstruction, which can be done as a single procedure where a fixed-volume silicone implant is inserted at the same time as the mastectomy. Or it can be a two-stage process where a temporary tissue expander is first inserted and expanded over time before being replaced with a permanent silicone implant. Another option is delayed reconstruction, where a tissue expander is placed later through the mastectomy scar, gradually inflated, and then potentially replaced with a permanent implant. The reconstruction approach will depend on your individual situation and preferences discussed with your surgical team.

question: Are breast implants safe for breast reconstruction?

However, it's important to be aware of the potential risks. Two very rare types of cancer, breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL) and breast implant-associated squamous cell carcinoma (BIA-SCC), have been found in a very small number of women with breast implants. The most common symptom is a swelling around the implant and breast. If you develop a lump or swelling around your implant, even years later, contact your GP or treatment team right away to get it checked out. In most cases, these rare conditions can be treated successfully by removing the implant. Your treatment team will discuss the risks with you if you're considering implants.

question: How is breast reconstruction using a patient's own tissue performed?

Breast reconstruction using your own tissue involves taking skin, fat, and sometimes muscle from another part of your body (called the donor site) and using it to create the new breast shape. There are two main techniques for this type of reconstruction:

2. Pedicled flap reconstruction: The tissue from the donor site remains attached to its original blood supply. The flap of tissue and its blood supply are then moved to the chest area to form the new breast shape.

The key is ensuring the reconstructed breast has a good blood supply from the beginning. Your surgeon will carefully plan the procedure to give you the best possible outcome.

question: Why is having a good blood supply important for breast reconstruction?

In the first few days after surgery, the new breast will be closely monitored to check that the blood supply is sufficient and the tissue remains healthy.

If there are any issues with poor blood flow, you may need an additional operation to try to improve the blood supply. In some cases, partial or complete loss of the reconstructed breast can occur if the blood supply is not adequate, although this is rare. Your surgeon will discuss these potential risks with you.

question: What is fat transfer (lipomodelling) and how is it used in breast reconstruction?
derived_answer: Fat transfer, also known as lipomodelling, is a technique that involves taking fat from one area of the body, such as the tummy, thighs, or lower back, and injecting it into the breast area. This procedure can be used for several purposes related to breast reconstruction:  - After breast-conserving surgery, it can help improve the appearance of the remaining breast. - After breast reconstruction with implants, lipomodelling can adjust the size or shape of the reconstructed breast, or help hide visible rippling from the implant. - Before delayed breast reconstruction, it may be done after a mastectomy and radiotherapy to improve the condition of the skin in preparation for reconstruction. - In some cases, lipomodelling alone can be used to reconstruct a breast without implants.  The fat transfer procedure is typically done under general anesthesia as an outpatient procedure, although local anesthesia is sometimes used. Multiple sessions may be needed to achieve the desired breast shape and appearance. While recovery is usually smooth, you can expect some bruising, swelling, and pain at the areas where fat was removed, as well as small scars.

question: What options are available for reconstructing the nipple after a mastectomy?
derived_answer: If it's not possible to keep your natural nipple during a mastectomy and breast reconstruction, there are a few options available for creating a new nipple. One option is nipple reconstruction surgery, where the surgeon uses part of the skin from your reconstructed breast to create a nipple. This is usually done several months after the initial reconstruction to allow the new breast to fully heal and settle into the correct position. Another option is nipple and areola tattooing, which can give a more natural appearance and match the opposite breast. Tattooing can be done alone to create the appearance of a nipple and areola, or in combination with surgical nipple reconstruction. The choice between these options is a personal decision based on your preferences and what you feel is the final step in your reconstruction journey.

question: What are some potential problems that can occur soon after breast reconstruction surgery?
derived_answer: After breast reconstruction surgery, some potential problems that can arise include bleeding, bruising, wound infection, and delayed wound healing. Bleeding can sometimes collect in the reconstructed breast, causing swelling, discomfort, and hardness, which is called a hematoma. If a large hematoma develops in the first few days, you may need an additional operation to stop the bleeding. Bruising to the reconstructed breast and areas where tissue was taken is common, but it usually goes away within a few weeks. Signs of a wound infection include tenderness, swelling, warmth, redness, fluid discharge, and feeling generally unwell with a fever. If you experience these, contact your healthcare provider right away as you may need antibiotics. In some cases, an infection around an implant may require its removal to allow the infection to fully resolve before considering further reconstruction. Delayed wound healing can also occur, sometimes taking longer than 6 weeks, and wounds can potentially reopen along the scar line. Factors like infection, diabetes, being overweight, and smoking can contribute to delayed healing.

question: What is a seroma and how is it treated?

While seromas can be uncomfortable, they are a common side effect and your medical team will monitor and treat them as needed.

question: What is the risk of tissue failure after flap reconstruction?

If the blood supply is not sufficient, the surgeon will need to remove the affected tissue. question: What is capsular contracture and what causes it?
derived_answer: Capsular contracture is a potential longer-term problem that can occur after implant reconstruction for breast cancer. After the implant is placed, a thin layer of scar tissue forms around it as part of the normal healing process. In some cases, this scar tissue capsule can tighten and harden around the implant, causing the breast to feel hard and potentially distorting its shape. Some people may also experience pain. Capsular contracture may be more likely in people who have had radiation therapy, infections, or are smokers.

question: How durable are breast implants and what happens if they leak?
derived_answer: Modern breast implants are designed to be very durable. The implant linings are strong, and the silicone gel inside is firm, which makes the risk of leaks and tears quite small. If you can feel a lump or if a scan shows the implant is damaged, you will likely need to have the implant surgically removed and replaced. It's important to notify your doctor, surgeon, or breast care nurse right away if you notice any changes in the shape, discomfort, or swelling of your reconstructed breast.

question: What is a hernia and how can it occur after breast reconstruction surgery?

question: What are hypertrophic and keloid scars?

These types of scars can take several years to settle and improve in appearance. Keloid scars are similar but more severe - they continue to grow beyond the original wound area and can cover normal tissue even after healing is complete. Keloid scars can be painful, tender and itchy. If you develop concerning scar issues, let your medical team know so they can evaluate and recommend appropriate treatment.

question: Will I need to get mammograms after breast reconstruction surgery?

derived_answer: It's common to be called back for additional tests after your first mammogram, even if there's no sign of breast cancer. question: What happens during a breast clinic appointment?
derived_answer: During a breast clinic appointment, you may first need to fill out a short questionnaire about your family history of breast problems, any medications you're taking (like hormone replacement therapy or birth control pills), previous breast surgeries, and any other existing health conditions. After that, you'll have a breast examination where a doctor or nurse will physically check your breasts. You may also undergo further tests like breast imaging (x-ray or scan to produce images of the inside of your breasts) or a biopsy (removing a small amount of breast tissue to examine under a microscope). The specific order of tests can vary between clinics. Having a breast exam, imaging, and biopsy together is known as a 'triple assessment' which may be necessary for diagnosis, but you may not need all three tests.

question: What is a mammogram and how is it performed?
derived_answer: A mammogram is a breast x-ray used to examine breast tissue. During the mammogram, a female mammographer (an expert in taking breast x-rays) will explain the process and answer any questions you have. You will need to remove your clothing from the waist up and stand in front of the mammography machine. Your breasts will be placed one at a time on the x-ray machine and pressed down firmly with a clear plate. At least two pictures (x-rays) will be taken of each breast from different angles to capture all the breast tissue, including the area extending into your armpit. Be sure to let the mammographer know if you are or may be pregnant.

question: What is a 3D mammogram or tomosynthesis?
derived_answer: A 3D mammogram, also known as digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT), is a more detailed type of mammogram used in some hospitals. It creates 3D images of the breast using lower dose X-rays. The breast is positioned the same way as a regular mammogram, but the X-ray arm rotates and curves around the breast, taking multiple pictures from different angles. These images are then combined by a computer to create 3D images, which can make it easier to see overlapping breast tissue.

question: What do the letter and number codes mean when describing breast imaging results?
derived_answer:
When describing breast imaging results, you may hear them referred to using a letter and number code. 'M' stands for mammogram results, while 'U' stands for ultrasound results. The numbers indicate the findings:

M1/U1 = Normal breast tissue
M2/U2 = Benign (not cancer)
M3/U3 = Uncertain but probably benign 
M4/U4 = Suspicious and possibly cancer
M5/U5 = Cancer

So for example, 'M4' would mean the mammogram results look suspicious for possible cancer.
